n:
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “slain [one].” The term חָלָל (khalal) suggests something other than a natural death (cf. {{Numbers 19:16|Num 19:16}}; {{Numbers 23:24|23:24}}; Jer 51:52; {{Ezekiel 26:15|Ezek 26:15}}; {{Ezekiel 30:24|30:24}}; {{Ezekiel 31:17|31:17-18}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text includes “to possess it,” but this has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “struck,” but in context a fatal blow is meant; cf. NLT “who committed the murder.”

*Translator's note:* The combination “a wadi with flowing water” is necessary because a wadi (נַחַל, nakhal) was ordinarily a dry stream or riverbed. For this ritual, however, a perennial stream must be chosen so that there would be fresh, rushing water.

*Study note:* The unworked heifer, fresh stream, and uncultivated valley speak of ritual purity—of freedom from human contamination.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the priests, the sons of Levi.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the name of the Lord.” See note on {{Deuteronomy 10:8|Deut 10:8}}. The pronoun has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by their mouth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “every controversy and every blow.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “slain [one].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wadi,” a seasonal watercourse through a valley.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “our eyes.” This is a figure of speech known as synecdoche in which the part (the eyes) is put for the whole (the entire person).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “seen”; the implied object (the crime committed) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Atone for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and do not place innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the eyes of” (so ASV, NASB, NIV).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the prisoners.” The pronoun has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.

*Study note:* This requirement for the woman to *shave her head* may symbolize the putting away of the old life and customs in preparation for being numbered among the people of the Lord. The same is true for the two following requirements.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “she is to…remove the clothing of her captivity” (cf. NASB); NRSV “discard her captive’s garb.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sit”; KJV, NASB, NRSV “remain.”

*Translator's note:* The verb בּוֹא (boʾ; “to come”) with the preposition אֶל (ʾel; “to”) means “to approach, to come to” (*HALOT* 113 s.v. בּוֹא) and is a euphemism for coming together for sexual relations. A clearer euphemism has been used for the translation than the more literal “get together with.” See the note at {{2 Samuel 12:24|2 Sam 12:24}} on this phrase being only a euphemism.

*Study note:* *Heb* “send her off.” The Hebrew term שִׁלַּחְתָּה (shillakhtah) is a somewhat euphemistic way of referring to divorce, the matter clearly in view here (cf. {{Deuteronomy 22:19|Deut 22:19}}, {{Deuteronomy 22:29|29}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:1|24:1}}, {{Deuteronomy 24:3|3}}; Jer 3:1; {{Malachi 2:16|Mal 2:16}}). This passage does not have the matter of divorce as its principal objective, so it should not be understood as endorsing divorce generally. It merely makes the point that if grounds for divorce exist (see {{Deuteronomy 24:1|Deut 24:1-4}}), and then divorce ensues, the husband could in no way gain profit from it.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which the translation indicates by the words “in any case.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text includes “for money.” This phrase has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “must not enslave her” (cf. ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT); *Heb* “[must not] be tyrannical over.”

*Study note:* *You have humiliated her*. Since divorce was considered rejection, the wife subjected to it would “lose face” in addition to the already humiliating event of having become a wife by force ({{Deuteronomy 21:11|21:11-13}}). Furthermore, the Hebrew verb translated “humiliated” here (עָנָה, ʿanah), commonly used to speak of rape (cf. {{Genesis 34:2|Gen 34:2}}; {{2 Samuel 13:12|2 Sam 13:12}}, {{2 Samuel 13:14|14}}, {{2 Samuel 13:22|22}}, {{2 Samuel 13:32|32}}; {{Judges 19:24|Judg 19:24}}), likely has sexual overtones as well. The woman may not be enslaved or abused after the divorce because it would be double humiliation (see also E. H. Merrill, *Deuteronomy* [NAC], 291).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one whom he loves and one whom he hates.” For the idea of שָׂנֵא (saneʾ, “hate”) meaning to be rejected or loved less (cf. NRSV “disliked”), see {{Genesis 29:31|Gen 29:31}}, {{Genesis 29:33|33}}; {{Malachi 1:2|Mal 1:2-3}}. Cf. A. Konkel, *NIDOTTE* 3:1256-60.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “both the one whom he loves and the one whom he hates.” On the meaning of the phrase “one whom he loves and one whom he hates” see the note on the word “other” earlier in this verse. The translation has been simplified for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when he causes his sons to inherit what is his.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the hated.”

*Translator's note:* See note on the word “other” in v. {{Deuteronomy 21:15|15}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “measure of two.” The Hebrew expression פִּי שְׁנַיִם (pi shenayim) suggests a two-thirds split; that is, the elder gets two parts and the younger one part. Cf. {{2 Kings 2:9|2 Kgs 2:9}}; Zech 13:8. The practice is implicit in Isaac’s blessing of Jacob ({{Genesis 25:31|Gen 25:31-34}}) and Jacob’s blessing of Ephraim ({{Genesis 48:8|Gen 48:8-22}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his generative power” (אוֹן, ʾon; cf. *HALOT* 22 s.v.). Cf. NAB “the firstfruits of his manhood”; NRSV “the first issue of his virility.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he does not listen to them.”

*Text-critical note:* The LXX and Smr read “to the men,” probably to conform to this phrase in v. {{Deuteronomy 21:21|21}}. However, since judicial cases were the responsibility of the elders in such instances (cf. {{Deuteronomy 19:12|Deut 19:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 21:3|21:3}}, {{Deuteronomy 21:6|6}}; {{Deuteronomy 25:7|25:7-8}}) the reading of the MT is likely original and correct here.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term בִּעַרְתָּה (biʿartah), here and elsewhere in such contexts (cf. {{Deuteronomy 13:5|Deut 13:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:7|17:7}}, {{Deuteronomy 17:12|12}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:19|19:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 21:9|21:9}}), suggests God’s anger which consumes like fire (thus בָּעַר, baʿar, “to burn”). See H. Ringgren, *TDOT* 2:203-4.

*Text-critical note:* Some LXX traditions read הַנִּשְׁאָרִים (hannishʾarim, “those who remain”) for the MT’s יִשְׂרָאֵל (yisraʾel, “Israel”), understandable in light of {{Deuteronomy 19:20|Deut 19:20}}. However, the more difficult reading found in the MT is more likely original.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which the translation indicates by “make certain.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hung,” but this could convey the wrong image in English (hanging with a rope as a means of execution). Cf. NCV “anyone whose body is displayed on a tree.”

*Study note:* The idea behind the phrase *cursed by God* seems to be not that the person was impaled because he was cursed but that to leave him exposed there was to invite the curse of God upon the whole land. Why this would be so is not clear, though the rabbinic idea that even a criminal is created in the image of God may give some clue (thus J. H. Tigay, *Deuteronomy* [JPSTC], 198). Paul cites this text (see Gal 3:13) to make the point that Christ, suspended from a cross, thereby took upon himself the curse associated with such a display of divine wrath and judgment (T. George, *Galatians* [NAC], 238-39).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you must not see,” but, if translated literally into English, the statement is misleading.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brother’s” (also later in this verse). In this context it is not limited to one’s siblings, however; cf. NAB “your kinsman’s.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hide yourself.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which the translation indicates with the words “without fail.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your brother” (also later in this verse).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is not.” The idea of “residing” is implied.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you do not know him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it”; the referent (the ox or sheep mentioned in v. {{Deuteronomy 22:1|1}}) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your brother” (also in v. {{Deuteronomy 22:4|4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you must not hide yourself.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you must not see.” See note at {{Deuteronomy 22:1|22:1}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and (must not) hide yourself from them.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which the translation indicates with “be sure.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “help him to lift them up.” In keeping with English style the singular is used in the translation, and the referent (“the animal”) has been specified for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man’s clothing.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term תּוֹעֵבָה (toʿevah, “offense”) speaks of anything that runs counter to ritual or moral order, especially (in the OT) to divine standards. Cross-dressing in this covenant context may suggest homosexuality, fertility cult ritual, or some other forbidden practice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the mother sitting upon the chicks or the eggs.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “over the chicks.” The preposition עַל is indicating the position the mother is in when she might be taken.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sons,” used here in a generic sense for offspring.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which the translation seeks to reflect with “be sure.”

*Translator's note:* Or “a parapet” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV); KJV “a battlement”; NLT “a barrier.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that you not place bloodshed in your house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “set apart.” The verb קָדַשׁ (qadash) in the Qal verbal stem (as here) has the idea of being holy or being treated with special care. Some take the meaning as “be off-limits, forfeited,” i.e., the total produce of the vineyard, both crops and grapes, have to be forfeited to the sanctuary (cf. {{Exodus 29:37|Exod 29:37}}; {{Exodus 30:29|30:29}}; Lev 6:18, 27; {{Numbers 16:37|Num 16:37-38}}; {{Haggai 2:12|Hag 2:12}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term שַׁעַטְנֵז (shaʿatnez) occurs only here and in Lev 19:19. *HALOT* 1610-11 s.v. takes it to be a contraction of words (שַׁשׁ [shash, “headdress”] and עַטְנַז [ʿatnaz, “strong”]). BDB 1043 s.v. שַׁעַטְנֵז offers the translation “mixed stuff” (cf. NEB “woven with two kinds of yarn”; NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT “woven together”). The general meaning is clear even if the etymology is not.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “twisted threads” (גְּדִלִים, gedilim) appears to be synonymous with צִיצִת (tsitsit) which, in {{Numbers 15:38|Num 15:38}}, occurs in a passage instructing Israel to remember the covenant. Perhaps that is the purpose of the tassels here as well. Cf. KJV, ASV “fringes”; NAB “twisted cords.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “goes to her,” a Hebrew euphemistic idiom for sexual relations. See note at {{Deuteronomy 21:13|Deut 21:13}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hate.” See note on the word “other” in {{Deuteronomy 21:15|Deut 21:15}}. Cf. NAB “comes to dislike”; NASB “turns against”; TEV “decides he doesn’t want.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “deeds of things”; NRSV “makes up charges against her”; NIV “slanders her.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brings against her a bad name”; NIV “gives her a bad name.”

*Translator's note:* The expression קָרַב אֶל (qarav ʾel) means “draw near to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for the intended purpose of sexual relations.
*Study note:* In light of v. {{Deuteronomy 22:17|17}} this would evidently be blood-stained sheets indicative of the first instance of intercourse. See E. H. Merrill, *Deuteronomy* (NAC), 302-3.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hated.” See note on the word “other” in {{Deuteronomy 21:15|Deut 21:15}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for he”; the referent (the man who made the accusation) has been specified in the translation to avoid confusion with the young woman’s father, the last-mentioned male.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brought forth a bad name.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term נְבָלָה (nevalah) means more than just something stupid. It refers to a moral lapse so serious as to jeopardize the whole covenant community (cf. {{Genesis 34:7|Gen 34:7}}; {{Judges 19:23|Judg 19:23}}; {{Judges 20:6|20:6}}, {{Judges 20:10|10}}; Jer 29:23). See C. Pan, *NIDOTTE* 3:11-13. Cf. NAB “she committed a crime against Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “burn.” See note on {{Deuteronomy 21:21|Deut 21:21}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lying down with.” The verb שָׁכַב (shakhav) “to lie down” can be a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a woman married to a husband.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “burn.” See note on the phrase “purge out” in {{Deuteronomy 21:21|Deut 21:21}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “finds.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lies down with,” a euphemism for going to bed for sexual relations.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “humbled.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wife.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “burn.” See note on the phrase “purge out” in {{Deuteronomy 21:21|Deut 21:21}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “found,” also in vv. {{Deuteronomy 22:27|27}}, {{Deuteronomy 22:28|28}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lay with” here refers to a forced sexual relationship, as the accompanying verb “seized” (חָזַק, khazaq) makes clear.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the man who lay with her, only him.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the man who attacked the woman) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The verb תָּפַשׂ (taphas) means “to sieze, grab.” In all other examples this action is done against another person’s will, as in being captured, arrested, attacked, or grabbed with insistence (e.g. {{1 Samuel 23:26|1 Sam 23:26}}; {{1 Kings 13:4|1 Kgs 13:4}}; {{1 Kings 18:40|18:40}}; {{2 Kings 14:13|2 Kgs 14:13}}; {{2 Kings 25:6|25:6}}; {{Isaiah 3:6|Isa 3:6}}; Jer 26:8; 34:3; 37:13; 52:9; {{Psalm 71:11|Ps 71:11}}; 2 Chr 25:23.) So it may be that the man is forcing himself on her, which is what leads the NIV to translate the next verb as “rape,” although it is a neutral euphemism for sexual relations. However, this is the only case where the object of תָּפַשׂ is a woman and the verb also also refers to holding or handling objects such as musical instruments, weapons, or scrolls. So it possible that it has a specialized, but otherwise unattested nuance regarding sexual or romantic relations, as is true of other expressions. Several contextual clues point away from rape and toward a consensual relationship. (1) The verb which seems to express force is different from the verb of force in the rape case in v. {{Deuteronomy 22:25|25}}. (2) The context distinguishes consequences based on whether the girl cried out, an expression of protest and a basis for distinguishing consent or force. But this case law does not mention her outcry which would have clarified a forcible act. While part of what is unique in this case is that the girl is not engaged, it is reasonable to expect the issue of consent to continue to apply. (3) The penalty is less than that of a man who slanders his new wife and certainly less than the sentence for rape. (4) The expression “and they are discovered” at the end of v. {{Deuteronomy 22:28|28}} uses the same wording as the expression in v. {{Deuteronomy 22:22|22}} which involves a consensual act. (5) Although from a separate context, the account of the rape of Dinah seems to express the Pentateuch’s negative attitude toward forcible rape, not in advocating for Simeon and Levi’s actions, but in the condemnation included in the line {{Genesis 34:7|Gen 34:7}} “because he has done a disgraceful thing in Israel.” This is very like the indictment in v. {{Deuteronomy 22:21|21}} against the consenting woman, “because she has done a disgraceful thing in Israel.” (6) The penalty of not being allowed to divorce her sounds like v. {{Deuteronomy 22:19|19}}, where the man is punished for disgracing his wife unfairly. His attempted divorce fails and he must provide for her thereafter (the probable point of not being allowed to divorce her.) Here too, if his holding her is not forced, but instead he has seduced her, he is not allowed to claim that his new wife is not pure (since he is the culprit) and so he must take responsibility for her, cannot divorce her, and must provide for her as a husband thereafter.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lies with.”

*Study note:* Beginning with 22:30, the verse numbers through 23:25 in the English Bible differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (*BHS*), with 22:30 ET = 23:1 HT, 23:1 ET = 23:2 HT, 23:2 ET = 23:3 HT, etc., through 23:25 ET = 23:26 HT. With 24:1 the verse numbers in the ET and HT are again the same.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “take.” In context this refers to marriage, as in the older English expression “take a wife.”

*Study note:* This presupposes either the death of the father or their divorce since it would be impossible for one to marry his stepmother while his father was still married to her.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “uncover his father’s skirt” (so ASV, NASB). This appears to be a circumlocution for describing the dishonor that would come to a father by having his own son share his wife’s sexuality (cf. NAB, NIV “dishonor his father’s bed”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bruised by crushing,” which many English versions take to refer to crushed testicles (NAB, NRSV, NLT); TEV “who has been castrated.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cut off with respect to the penis”; KJV, ASV “hath his privy member cut off”; English versions vary in their degree of euphemism here; cf. NAB, NRSV, TEV, NLT “penis”; NASB “male organ”; NCV “sex organ”; CEV “private parts”; NIV “emasculated by crushing or cutting.”

*Study note:* The Hebrew term translated “assembly” (קָהָל, qahal) does not refer here to the nation as such but to the formal services of the tabernacle or temple.

*Translator's note:* Or “a person born of an illegitimate marriage.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “enter the assembly of the Lord.” The phrase “do so” has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons to avoid redundancy.

*Study note:* *An Ammonite or Moabite*. These descendants of Lot by his two daughters (cf. {{Genesis 19:30|Gen 19:30-38}}) were thereby the products of incest and therefore excluded from the worshiping community. However, these two nations also failed to show proper hospitality to Israel on their way to Canaan (v. {{Deuteronomy 23:4|4}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term translated “ever” (עַד־עוֹלָם, ʿad ʿolam) suggests that “tenth generation” (vv. {{Deuteronomy 23:2|2}}, {{Deuteronomy 23:3|3}}) also means “forever.” However, in the OT sense “forever” means not “for eternity” but for an indeterminate future time. See A. Tomasino, *NIDOTTE* 3:346.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “enter the assembly of the Lord.” The phrase “do so” has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord your God changed.” The phrase “the Lord your God” has not been included in the translation here for stylistic reasons to avoid redundancy. Moreover, use of the pronoun “he” could create confusion regarding the referent (the Lord or Balaam).

*Translator's note:* The verb אָהֵב (ʾahev, “love”) here and commonly elsewhere in the Book of Deuteronomy speaks of God’s elective grace toward Israel. See note on the word “loved” in {{Deuteronomy 4:37|Deut 4:37}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brother.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sojourner.”

*Study note:* The same term ger (גֵּר) is used for the resident foreigner living in Israel and of the Israelite who lived in Egypt, despite the very different social conditions of each. A foreign resident has differing status in different countries. The Israelites were slaves in Egypt, but the resident foreigner in Israel was under the same laws (civil and religious) as the Israelite and could worship the Lord as part of the covenant community. Several passages emphasize equal standing under Mosaic Law ({{Exodus 12:49|Exod 12:49}}; Lev 24:22; {{Numbers 9:14|Num 9:14}}; {{Numbers 15:15|15:15}}, {{Numbers 15:16|16}}, {{Numbers 15:26|26}}, {{Numbers 15:29|29}}; {{Numbers 19:10|19:10}}; {{Numbers 35:15|35:15}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:16|Deut 1:16}}) or similar obligations ({{Exodus 20:10|Exod 20:10}}; {{Exodus 23:12|23:12}}; Lev 16:29; 17:10, 12, 13; 18:26; 24:16; {{Numbers 15:14|Num 15:14}}).

*Study note:* Concessions were made to the Edomites and Egyptians (as compared to the others listed in vv. {{Deuteronomy 23:1|1-6}}) because the Edomites (i.e., Esauites) were full “brothers” of Israel and the Egyptians had provided security and sustenance for Israel for more than four centuries.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “evil.” The context makes clear that this is a matter of ritual impurity, not moral impurity, so it is “evil” in the sense that it disbars one from certain religious activity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “nocturnal happening.” The Hebrew term קָרֶה (qareh) merely means “to happen” so the phrase here is euphemistic (a “night happening”) for some kind of bodily emission such as excrement or semen. Such otherwise normal physical functions rendered one ritually unclean whether accidental or not. See Lev 15:16-18; 22:4.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so that one may go outside there.” This expression is euphemistic.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sit.” This expression is euphemistic.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with it”; the referent (the spade mentioned at the beginning of the verse) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “what comes from you,” a euphemism.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “give [over] your enemies.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “nakedness of a thing”; NLT “any shameful thing.” The expression עֶרְוַת דָּבָר (ʿervat davar) refers specifically to sexual organs and, by extension, to any function associated with them. There are some aspects of human life that are so personal and private that they ought not be publicly paraded. Cultically speaking, even God is offended by such impropriety (cf. {{Genesis 9:22|Gen 9:22-23}}; Lev 18:6-12, 16-19; 20:11, 17-21). See B. Seevers, *NIDOTTE* 3:528-30.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text includes “from his master,” but this would be redundant in English style.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term translated “sacred prostitute” here (קְדֵשָׁה [qedeshah], from קַדֵשׁ [qadesh, “holy”]; cf. NIV “shrine prostitute”; NASB “cult prostitute”; NRSV, TEV, NLT “temple prostitute”) refers to the pagan fertility cults that employed female and male prostitutes in various rituals designed to evoke agricultural and even human fecundity (cf. {{Genesis 38:21|Gen 38:21-22}}; {{1 Kings 14:24|1 Kgs 14:24}}; {{1 Kings 15:12|15:12}}; {{1 Kings 22:47|22:47}}; {{2 Kings 23:7|2 Kgs 23:7}}; Hos 4:14). The Hebrew term for a regular, noncultic (i.e., “secular”) female prostitute is זוֹנָה (zonah).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “daughters.”

*Translator's note:* The male cultic prostitute was called קָדֵשׁ (qadesh; see note on the phrase “sacred prostitute” earlier in this verse). The colloquial Hebrew term for a “secular” male prostitute (i.e., a sodomite) is the disparaging epithet כֶּלֶב (kelev, “dog”) which occurs in the following verse (cf. KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sons.”

*Translator's note:* Here the Hebrew term זוֹנָה (zonah) refers to a noncultic (i.e., “secular”) female prostitute; see note on the phrase “sacred prostitute” in v. {{Deuteronomy 23:17|17}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of a dog.” This is the common Hebrew term for a noncultic (i.e., “secular”) male prostitute. See note on the phrase “sacred male prostitute” in v. {{Deuteronomy 23:17|17}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to your brother” (likewise in the following verse). Since this is not limited to actual siblings, “fellow Israelite” is used in the translation (cf. NAB, NASB “countrymen”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord your God.” The pronoun has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which is reflected in the translation by “surely.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it will be a sin to you”; NIV, NCV, NLT “be guilty of sin.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “grapes according to your appetite, your fullness.”

*Study note:* This is the so-called “levirate” custom (from the Latin term *levir*, “brother-in-law”), an ancient provision whereby a man who died without male descendants to carry on his name could have a son by proxy, that is, through a surviving brother who would marry his widow and whose first son would then be attributed to the brother who had died. This is the only reference to this practice in an OT legal text but it is illustrated in the story of Judah and his sons ({{Genesis 38|Gen 38}}) and possibly in the account of Ruth and Boaz ({{Ruth 2:8|Ruth 2:8}}; {{Ruth 3:12|3:12}}; {{Ruth 4:6|4:6}}).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “your heads, your tribes.” The Syriac presupposes either “heads of your tribes” or “your heads, your judges,” etc. (reading שֹׁפְטֵכֶם [shofetekhem] for שִׁבְטֵיכֶם [shivtekhem]). Its comparative difficulty favors the originality of the MT reading. Cf. KJV “your captains of your tribes”; NRSV “the leaders of your tribes”; NLT “your tribal leaders.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your.”

*Study note:* The ger (גֵּר) “foreign resident” here enters into the covenant with the community if Israel. Elsewhere in Mosaic Law the ger make sacrifices to the Lord (Lev 17:8; 22:18; {{Numbers 15:14|Num 15:14}}) and participate in Israel’s religious festivals: Passover {{Exodus 12:48|Exod 12:48}}; Day of Atonement Lev 16:29; Feast of Weeks {{Deuteronomy 16:10|Deut 16:10-14}}; Feast of Tabernacles/Temporary Shelters {{Deuteronomy 31:12|Deut 31:12}}. Several passages emphasize equal standing under Mosaic Law ({{Exodus 12:49|Exod 12:49}}; Lev 24:22; {{Numbers 9:14|Num 9:14}}; {{Numbers 15:15|15:15}}, {{Numbers 15:16|16}}, {{Numbers 15:26|26}}, {{Numbers 15:29|29}}; {{Numbers 19:10|19:10}}; {{Numbers 35:15|35:15}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:16|Deut 1:16}} or similar obligations {{Exodus 20:10|Exod 20:10}}; {{Exodus 23:12|23:12}}; Lev 16:29; 17:10, 12, 13; 18:26; 24:16; {{Numbers 15:14|Num 15:14}}. In many respects these ger (גֵּר) appear to be naturalized citizens who could not own land (land was allotted by tribe).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term שִׁקּוּץ (shiqquts) refers to anything out of keeping with the nature and character of Yahweh and therefore to be avoided by his people Israel. It is commonly used with or as a synonym for תּוֹעֵבָה (toʿevah, “detestable, abhorrent”; {{2 Kings 23:13|2 Kgs 23:13}}; Jer 16:18; {{Ezekiel 5:11|Ezek 5:11}}; {{Ezekiel 7:20|7:20}}; {{Ezekiel 11:18|11:18}}, {{Ezekiel 11:21|21}}; see note on the term “abhorrent” in {{Deuteronomy 7:25|Deut 7:25}}). See M. Grisanti, *NIDOTTE* 4:243-46.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the watered with the parched.” The word “ground” is implied. The exact meaning of the phrase is uncertain although it appears to be figurative. This appears to be a proverbial observation employing a figure of speech (a merism) suggesting totality. That is, the Israelite who violates the letter and even spirit of the covenant will harm not only himself but everything he touches—“the watered and the parched.” Cf. CEV “you will cause the rest of Israel to be punished along with you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the wrath of the Lord and his zeal.” The expression is a hendiadys, a figure in which the second noun becomes adjectival to the first.

*Study note:* To this point in the chapter, Moses has addressed the people with the singular pronoun “you,” but here he switches to the plural. Rhetorically, the singular pronoun has emphasized the responsibilities and consequences for the nation as a whole. It is a group responsibility that requires a group effort. At v. {{Deuteronomy 30:18|18}} he shifts to using the plural form. This individualizes the threatened punishment in v. {{Deuteronomy 30:18|18}} and highlights individual responsibility in the first half of v. {{Deuteronomy 30:19|19}} (calling heaven and earth as witness “against you”) before returning to the collective responsibility that “you” (singular) choose life.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis, which the translation indicates with “certainly.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to go there to possess it.”

*Translator's note:* The words “I also call on you” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. In the Hebrew text vv. {{Deuteronomy 30:19|19-20}} are one long sentence, which the translation divides into two.
